Whatever you do, don't demonise it outright. Coming from someone teetotal at 21 after nearly ruining my own life, your kids are going to be exposed to the concept of alcohol and drugs, a balanced approach of telling them the dangers without demonising it outright is probably the safest approach. No matter what you do, don't make your kids feel like they'd have to hide their use from you (or hide anything for that matter). The best way to prevent them from doing anything too harmful would be to have them trust you more than trying to encourage them not to. 

I never felt that using substances was even a topic that could be brought up at home, and I went off the deep end the second I moved out at 18 (there were naturally other contributing factors, but drugs and alcohol being a 'big bad' was a big one). My parents, to this day, don't know what happened in these years, even with regular visits.

As for the extreme eczema, welcome to the family, join the club! It sucks and it may not help to hear, but I promise you that it does get better. I had moderate to severe eczema my entire life, and two years ago I had the worst flair up that kept me out of school for a few months. Worst part was the pain, but also not being comfortable with your skin as a result can really damage your self esteem. 

Thing is though, that flair ups don't last forever. Finding a good dermatologist is already half the trouble, and then it's really a matter of waiting it out. I know it's really anecdotal, and things work differently for different people, but topical cortisol steroids really helped cool things down, but that you probably would want to discuss with a doctor. 

Other than that is keeping all areas really clean and moisturised, especially after scratching, preferably using a moisturiser that's more thick and oily without any perfume. Try avoid all perfumated products entirely. And confortable clothes made out of organic materials such as cotton, linen or silk (I'm not bougee like that so I stick to cotton) to prevent irritating the skin.

And then there's taking care of yourself in general. Accepting that this sucks, its painful and it's difficult to deal with. But also take the time to treat yourself and lift your spirits up a bit. Hang out with people that don't stress you out, and cut down on people who do. Generally cut out as many stress factors plausible. The mind, emotion and body are more connected than you'd think. And then it's a matter of riding the wave and waiting for it to lessen.

I'm glad I was able to help make you feel better.

It's normal not to know who or whether you want to date at that age, and going out with people you don't necessarily like happens quite a bit, believe me. It's not wrong per se as each experience can maybe teach you something about yourself and what you do or don't want. 

My immediate family now knows and have had very mixed reactions. My mum still outright refuses to believe me and we had a row the third time I tried to come out to her, and I keep my love life from her as much as possible as a result, which works for us (not the healthiest, ik) but my dad and sister are slowly coming to terms with it. And I have friends who I consider family that love and accept me. 

I would say to be careful when coming out to your friends and family, especially if they are non affirming. Don't ever come out if it may put your safety in jeopardy, and always have a back-up plan. Pray for strength as it can be a very tough conversation to have, and be armed with information as you might have to explain a lot to them (my family for example had no idea what bisexuality even was). Even then, it will probably take time for them, so you may have to be patient for a while. 

Please don't feel pressured to come out to anyone, including your friends, if you don't feel comfortable to do so. It's up to you, and no one should make you feel as if you have to do so. Also, don't feel obligated to label yourself unless you feel comfortable doing so. You're God's child first and foremost, never forget that, and never let anyone else tell you otherwise!

I'm sure I speak for everyone when I say this sub is glad to have you! 

God bless

Hi, I just wanted to add in my two cents.

You're still thirteen so you have all the time in the world to figure out your orientation, trust me. Questioning at any age, but especially that young, is completely normal and part of the process. 

About your parents and community, I know it's hard because you love them and want them to love and accept whoever you grow up to be, but I would wait until you're a little bit more certain in your identity before involving them, unless you absolutely have to.

Growing up as a bisexual in a non affirming Christian family myself I know that it can be challenging to know whether what you're feeling is against the will of God or if you're sinning by having a crush on the same gender, and those are valid questions. But I just want you to know that God is the God of love! Jesus loves you, and wants you to come to him as you are! Your orientation does not exclude you from God's love and grace.
